Chapter 5. Building a New Vision: Toward Inclusive and Intersectional Feminism.
Over the years, it became more and more obvious—the old ways of thinking about feminism just weren’t cutting it. The movement had to evolve, to make space for voices and experiences that had been left out for far too long.
For Black women, this wasn’t just about being invited to the conversation. It was about claiming real leadership, stepping forward as visionaries who shape the future.
You know, the concept of intersectionality started to take root—even before anyone actually gave it a name. People began to realize you can’t separate race, gender, and class. For Black women, the struggle wasn’t just about facing sexism or racism in isolation, but about how those forces overlap and create challenges that are completely unique.
Picture a college student who’s drawn to the idea of feminism but feels frustrated because issues like poverty, police violence, or access to healthcare aren’t getting any attention. She starts to see that her own freedom is tied up with the freedom of others. That true liberation? It isn’t possible for one person unless it’s possible for everyone.
This new vision of feminism was really grounded in solidarity. It called for listening—really listening—to those whose voices had been overlooked. It meant being willing to challenge old assumptions and recognizing that the fight for justice is so much bigger than just individual rights. It’s about transforming the very systems that keep people divided and held back.
So many found inspiration in the strength of those who came before. Women who survived slavery, who organized for civil rights, who built families and entire communities against unimaginable odds. Their stories remind us—change can happen, even when it feels impossible.
Most people don’t realize just how powerful it is to simply speak the truth. To call out exactly how oppression works, and to imagine a world that’s better. Whether in classrooms, churches, or right there in someone’s living room, conversations started to shift. Folks began asking new questions, like—Whose voices are missing? Whose needs are going unheard? What would it look like to build a movement that truly includes everyone?
The work is far from finished, and that’s something we can’t ignore. But with every step forward, the vision gets a little clearer—a world where Black women are seen in all their complexity, where their challenges and victories matter, and where their liberation is recognized as essential for everyone.
